rationale: B wins by a hair because it adds a genuinely different, proof-driven trade wedge: "One retrofitted Sweetgreen, before and after the conveyor," and then has the discipline to say, "This angle does not exist until that data does." A is clean and useful, especially "Sweetgreen says automation lifts margins — its bottom line still says otherwise," but it mostly stops at the three obvious lanes: rollout, margin skepticism, and labor. B has one invented contextual flourish, but its unit-level follow-up and sharper proof gating make it more useful strategic material.
gaps_in_A: "Sweetgreen's own rollout is a concrete, citable case of reduced staff hours tied to automated assembly" overstates the record. The update says some people worry about reduced staff hours; it does not prove reductions have happened.
"Decay: 24hr" on the default-store-format angle underrates the trade runway. If Sweetgreen is changing most new-store builds, that can support more than announcement-day coverage.

It misses the strongest proof-shaped trade package: a named retrofit with before/after throughput, staffing, and margin. Without that, the rollout angle leans on chainwide claims and spokesperson confirmation.
gaps_in_B: "automation live mostly in pilots and demo units" is imported context, not in the update. Don't smuggle industry history into a blind angle set unless you source it.
"Story type: category-creation" is inflated. Sweetgreen is expanding an operating format; the facts do not show it is creating a category.
"This angle does not exist until that data does" is honest, but it also means the retrofit angle belongs in a conditional follow-up bucket, not on equal footing with current announcement-day angles.
"turn an exposé into a balanced piece" dramatizes the labor angle. The facts support staffing-risk questions, not an inevitable exposé.
